key_insight: Going beyond activation strength, the paper identifies which brain regions genuinely represent a visual concept by using interventions and counterfactual stimuli to test causal effects on neural responses.
problem_solved: Activation-based localization can be confounded by correlated visual or semantic cues; this work separates mere correlation from causal representation in the human visual brain.
method: Use activation-maximization to nominate candidate concept-selective regions from brain imaging data.
Generate controlled or counterfactual visual interventions (e.g., targeted edits or synthetic stimuli) that manipulate the target concept while holding correlated cues constant.

Apply causal tests / statistical causal discovery on region responses to determine whether manipulating the concept changes neural activity (evidence of representation) versus responses driven by confounds.
impact: Enables more rigorous mapping between visual concepts and brain regions, improving interpretability and evaluation of neural representations; informs AI models and attribution methods by providing a causal benchmark for what it means to 'represent' a concept.
visual_elements: Pipeline diagram: activation maximization → counterfactual stimulus generation → causal test → labeled region map
Before/after image pair showing targeted concept edits and corresponding change in brain activation heatmaps
Bar/line chart comparing region responses to original vs. intervened stimuli highlighting causal vs. correlational responses
Venn-style schematic distinguishing 'activated', 'correlated', and 'causally representing' region sets
paper_title: From Activation to Causality: Discovery of Causal Visual Representations in the Human Brain
paper_authors: Yuval Golbari, Navve Wasserman, Matias Cosarinsky, Roman Beliy, Aude Oliva
